passage: Under the neem tree at the village school, it was time to wash hands before the porridge. "No!" said Binita. She folded her arms and turned her back to the tap. Ramesh Sir did not raise his voice or call her name across the yard. "Hands next, then porridge. I will wait here," he said, the same words he used every day. Other children lined up at the tap. Binita peeked over her shoulder, then dragged her feet over and held out her hands. "Some days she still says no," he told the helper, "but it takes less time now."

qa.q: What was Binita told to do before the porridge?
qa.a: She had to wash her hands at the tap.

qa.q: What might Binita have been feeling when she peeked over her shoulder at the tap?
qa.a: She was probably unsure and curious, wanting to see whether Sir would give in or get cross; his calm waiting seemed to make her feel safe enough to come over.

qa.q: What did Ramesh Sir do that worked better than shaming her?
qa.a: He stayed calm and used the same firm words in the same order each day, without scolding her in front of others. The steady routine made giving in easier for her.

qa.q: How might the other children see Ramesh Sir's way of handling Binita?
qa.a: They probably see that Sir is fair and predictable, so rules feel safe. Nobody was embarrassed in front of them, which makes it easier for them to trust him too.

grounding: A child says no and turns away, and a calm firm routine reduces it better than shame.
